2019



2019 May/June · 9231/11 & 9231/12 · Question 2 · 5 marks
Let
\[
u_n=\frac{4\sin\left(n-\frac12\right)\sin\frac12}{\cos(2n-1)+\cos1}.
\]
(i) Show that \(u_n=\sec n-\sec(n-1)\). [2]
(ii) Use the method of differences to find \(\sum_{n=1}^{N}u_n\). [2]
(iii) Explain why \(u_1+u_2+u_3+\cdots\) does not converge. [1]


Show answer and mark scheme

(i) Using the sum-to-product identities,
\[
\cos(2n-1)+\cos1=2\cos n\cos(n-1),
\]
and
\[
2\sin\left(n-\frac12\right)\sin\frac12
=\cos(n-1)-\cos n.
\]
Therefore
\[
u_n
=\frac{2\{\cos(n-1)-\cos n\}}{2\cos n\cos(n-1)}
=\boxed{\sec n-\sec(n-1)}.
\]
(ii) Writing the first few and final terms,
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{N}u_n
=(\sec1-1)+(\sec2-\sec1)+\cdots+(\sec N-\sec(N-1))
=\boxed{\sec N-1}.
\]
(iii) The sequence \(\sec N\) does not approach a finite limit as \(N\to\infty\); in particular, \(\cos N\) oscillates and can be arbitrarily close to \(0\). Hence the sequence of partial sums \(\sec N-1\) has no limit, so the infinite series diverges.

 Completed

Sources: Cambridge International 9231/11/M/J/2019, Q2; 9231/12/M/J/2019, Q2.





2019 October/November · 9231/11, 9231/12 & 9231/13 · Question 5 · 9 marks
Let
\[
S_N=\sum_{r=1}^{N}(5r+1)(5r+6),
\qquad
T_N=\sum_{r=1}^{N}\frac1{(5r+1)(5r+6)}.
\]
(i) Use standard results to show that
\[
S_N=\frac13N(25N^2+90N+83).
\]
[3]
(ii) Use the method of differences to express \(T_N\) in terms of \(N\). [4]
(iii) Find \(\lim_{N\to\infty}\dfrac{S_NT_N}{N^3}\). [2]


Show answer and mark scheme

(i) Expanding the summand,
\[
S_N=\sum_{r=1}^{N}(25r^2+35r+6)
=25\sum_{r=1}^{N}r^2+35\sum_{r=1}^{N}r+6N.
\]
Substituting the standard results,
\[
S_N
=\frac{25}{6}N(N+1)(2N+1)
+\frac{35}{2}N(N+1)+6N
\]
\[
=\boxed{\frac13N(25N^2+90N+83)}.
\]
(ii) Partial fractions give
\[
\frac1{(5r+1)(5r+6)}
=\frac15\left(\frac1{5r+1}-\frac1{5r+6}\right),
\]
Hence
\[
T_N=\frac15\left[
\left(\frac16-\frac1{11}\right)
+\left(\frac1{11}-\frac1{16}\right)
+\cdots
+\left(\frac1{5N+1}-\frac1{5N+6}\right)
\right].
\]
All intermediate terms cancel, so
\[
\boxed{T_N=\frac1{30}-\frac1{5(5N+6)}}.
\]
(iii) From the leading terms,
\[
\frac{S_N}{N^3}\longrightarrow\frac{25}{3},
\qquad
T_N\longrightarrow\frac1{30}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{S_NT_N}{N^3}=\frac5{18}}.
\]

 Completed

Sources: Cambridge International 9231/11/O/N/2019, Q5; 9231/12/O/N/2019, Q5; 9231/13/O/N/2019, Q5.




2020



2020 May/June · 9231/11 & 9231/12 · Question 4 · 10 marks
(a) By first expressing \(1/(r^2-1)\) in partial fractions, show that
\[
\sum_{r=2}^{n}\frac1{r^2-1}
=\frac34-\frac{2n+1}{2n(n+1)}.
\]
[5]
(b) Deduce \(\sum_{r=2}^{3}\frac1{r^2-1}\). [1]
(c) Find \(\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{r=n+1}^{2n}\frac1{r^2-1}\). [4]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a) Since \(r^2-1=(r-1)(r+1)\),
\[
\frac1{r^2-1}
=\frac12\left(\frac1{r-1}-\frac1{r+1}\right).
\]
Therefore
\[
\sum_{r=2}^{n}\frac1{r^2-1}
=\frac12\left[
\left(1-\frac13\right)
+\left(\frac12-\frac14\right)
+\left(\frac13-\frac15\right)
+\cdots
+\left(\frac1{n-1}-\frac1{n+1}\right)
\right]
\]
\[
=\frac12\left(1+\frac12-\frac1n-\frac1{n+1}\right)
=\frac34-\frac{2n+1}{2n(n+1)},
\]
as required.
(b) Put \(n=3\) in part (a):
\[
\sum_{r=2}^{3}\frac1{r^2-1}=\boxed{\frac{11}{24}}.
\]
(c) Let \(F(n)=\sum_{r=2}^{n}1/(r^2-1)\). Then
\[
\sum_{r=n+1}^{2n}\frac1{r^2-1}=F(2n)-F(n).
\]
Using part (a),
\[
F(2n)-F(n)
=\left(\frac34-\frac{4n+1}{4n(2n+1)}\right)
-\left(\frac34-\frac{2n+1}{2n(n+1)}\right).
\]
Both remaining fractions tend to \(0\), so
\[
\boxed{0}.
\]

 Completed

Sources: Cambridge International 9231/11/M/J/2020, Q4; 9231/12/M/J/2020, Q4.





2020 May/June · 9231/13 · Question 3 · 8 marks
Let
\[
S_n=2^2+6^2+10^2+\cdots+(4n-2)^2.
\]
(a) Use standard results to show that
\[
S_n=\frac43n(4n^2-1).
\]
[4]
(b) Express \(n/S_n\) in partial fractions and find \(\sum_{n=1}^{N}n/S_n\). [4]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a)
\[
S_n=\sum_{r=1}^{n}(4r-2)^2
=\sum_{r=1}^{n}(16r^2-16r+4).
\]
Hence
\[
S_n
=\frac{16}{6}n(n+1)(2n+1)-8n(n+1)+4n
\]
\[
=\frac43n(4n^2-1),
\]
as required.
(b) Therefore
\[
\frac{n}{S_n}=\frac3{4(2n-1)(2n+1)}
=\frac38\left(\frac1{2n-1}-\frac1{2n+1}\right).
\]
Writing the terms explicitly,
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac{n}{S_n}
=\frac38\left[
\left(1-\frac13\right)
+\left(\frac13-\frac15\right)
+\cdots
+\left(\frac1{2N-1}-\frac1{2N+1}\right)
\right].
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{\sum_{n=1}^{N}\frac{n}{S_n}=\frac38\left(1-\frac1{2N+1}\right)
=\frac{3N}{4(2N+1)}}.
\]

 Completed

Source: Cambridge International 9231/13/M/J/2020, Q3.





2020 October/November · 9231/13 · Question 2 · 7 marks
(a) Use standard results to find
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}(7r+1)(7r+8)
\]
as a cubic polynomial in \(n\). [3]
(b) Use the method of differences to find
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac1{(7r+1)(7r+8)}.
\]
[4]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a) Since
\[
(7r+1)(7r+8)=49r^2+63r+8,
\]
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}(7r+1)(7r+8)
=49\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}6
+63\frac{n(n+1)}2+8n
\]
\[
=\boxed{\frac n3(49n^2+168n+143)}.
\]
(b) Partial fractions give
\[
\frac1{(7r+1)(7r+8)}
=\frac17\left(\frac1{7r+1}-\frac1{7r+8}\right),
\]
Hence
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac1{(7r+1)(7r+8)}
=\frac17\left[
\left(\frac18-\frac1{15}\right)
+\left(\frac1{15}-\frac1{22}\right)
+\cdots
+\left(\frac1{7n+1}-\frac1{7n+8}\right)
\right]
\]
\[
=\frac17\left(\frac18-\frac1{7n+8}\right),
\]
so
\[
\boxed{\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac1{(7r+1)(7r+8)}
=\frac n{8(7n+8)}}.
\]

 Completed

Sources: Cambridge International 9231/11/O/N/2020, Q2; 9231/13/O/N/2020, Q2.





2020 October/November · 9231/12 · Question 3 · 7 marks
(a) By simplifying
\[
(x^n-\sqrt{x^{2n}+1})(x^n+\sqrt{x^{2n}+1}),
\]
show that
\[
\frac1{x^n-\sqrt{x^{2n}+1}}=-x^n-\sqrt{x^{2n}+1}.
\]
[1]
Let
\[
u_n=x^{n+1}+\sqrt{x^{2n+2}+1}
+\frac1{x^n-\sqrt{x^{2n}+1}}.
\]
(b) Use the method of differences to find \(\sum_{n=1}^{N}u_n\). [3]
(c) Deduce the values of \(x\) for which the infinite series converges and give its sum. [3]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a) The product is a difference of two squares:
\[
(x^n-\sqrt{x^{2n}+1})(x^n+\sqrt{x^{2n}+1})
=x^{2n}-(x^{2n}+1)=-1.
\]
Dividing by \(x^n-\sqrt{x^{2n}+1}\) gives the stated identity.
(b) Using part (a),
\[
u_n=\left(x^{n+1}+\sqrt{x^{2n+2}+1}\right)
-\left(x^n+\sqrt{x^{2n}+1}\right).
\]
Thus the sum is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{n=1}^{N}u_n
={}&\left(x^2+\sqrt{x^4+1}-x-\sqrt{x^2+1}\right)\\
&+\left(x^3+\sqrt{x^6+1}-x^2-\sqrt{x^4+1}\right)+\cdots\\
&+\left(x^{N+1}+\sqrt{x^{2N+2}+1}-x^N-\sqrt{x^{2N}+1}\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
All intermediate terms cancel, giving
\[
\boxed{\sum_{n=1}^{N}u_n
=x^{N+1}+\sqrt{x^{2N+2}+1}-x-\sqrt{x^2+1}}.
\]
(c) A finite limit requires \(x^{N+1}\to0\), which occurs precisely when \(|x|<1\). Then
\[
\sqrt{x^{2N+2}+1}\longrightarrow1.
\]
Therefore the series converges for \(-1<x<1\), and its sum is
\[
\boxed{1-x-\sqrt{x^2+1}}.
\]

 Completed

Source: Cambridge International 9231/12/O/N/2020, Q3.




2021



2021 May/June · 9231/11 & 9231/12 · Question 2 · 9 marks
(a) Use standard results to find \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}(1-r-r^2)\). [3]
(b) Show that
\[
\frac{1-r-r^2}{(r^2+2r+2)(r^2+1)}
=\frac{r+1}{(r+1)^2+1}-\frac r{r^2+1},
\]
and hence find the corresponding sum from \(r=1\) to \(n\). [5]
(c) Deduce the sum to infinity. [1]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a)
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}(1-r-r^2)
=n-\frac{n(n+1)}2-\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}6
\]
\[
=\boxed{-\frac13n(n^2+3n-1)}.
\]
(b) Combining the fractions on the right gives
\[
\frac{(r+1)(r^2+1)-r\{(r+1)^2+1\}}
{\{(r+1)^2+1\}(r^2+1)}
=\frac{1-r-r^2}{(r^2+2r+2)(r^2+1)},
\]
which proves the identity. Therefore
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left[
\frac{r+1}{(r+1)^2+1}-\frac r{r^2+1}
\right]
\]
\[
=\left(\frac25-\frac12\right)
+\left(\frac3{10}-\frac25\right)
+\cdots
+\left(\frac{n+1}{(n+1)^2+1}-\frac n{n^2+1}\right).
\]
The intermediate terms cancel, giving
\[
\boxed{\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac{1-r-r^2}{(r^2+2r+2)(r^2+1)}
=\frac{n+1}{(n+1)^2+1}-\frac12}.
\]
(c) Since
\[
\frac{n+1}{(n+1)^2+1}\longrightarrow0,
\]
the sum to infinity is \(\boxed{-\frac12}\).

 Completed

Sources: Cambridge International 9231/11/M/J/2021, Q2; 9231/12/M/J/2021, Q2.





2021 May/June · 9231/13 · Question 1 · 6 marks
Let
\[
u_r=\frac1{\cos(r+1)\cos r}.
\]
(a) Express \(u_r\) as a difference involving tangents. [2]
(b) Use the method of differences to find \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}u_r\). [3]
(c) Explain why the infinite series does not converge. [1]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a) Since
\[
\tan(r+1)-\tan r=\frac{\sin1}{\cos(r+1)\cos r},
\]
\[
u_r=\frac{\tan(r+1)-\tan r}{\sin1}.
\]
(b) Therefore
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}u_r
=\frac1{\sin1}\{(\tan2-\tan1)+(\tan3-\tan2)+\cdots
+(\tan(n+1)-\tan n)\}.
\]
After cancellation,
\[
\boxed{\sum_{r=1}^{n}u_r=\frac{\tan(n+1)-\tan1}{\sin1}}.
\]
(c) The sequence \(\tan(n+1)\) does not approach a finite limit, so the partial sums have no limit. Hence the infinite series diverges.

 Completed

Source: Cambridge International 9231/13/M/J/2021, Q1.





2021 October/November · 9231/11 & 9231/13 · Question 2 · 8 marks
(a) Find \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}r(r+1)(r+2)\) in fully factorised form. [3]
(b) Express \(1/[r(r+1)(r+2)]\) in partial fractions and hence find its sum from \(r=1\) to \(n\). [5]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a) Expand and use the standard results:
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}r(r+1)(r+2)
=\sum_{r=1}^{n}(r^3+3r^2+2r)
\]
\[
=\left\{\frac{n(n+1)}2\right\}^2
+\frac12n(n+1)(2n+1)+n(n+1)
\]
\[
=\boxed{\frac14n(n+1)(n+2)(n+3)}.
\]
(b) Write
\[
\frac1{r(r+1)(r+2)}
=\frac12\left[\frac1{r(r+1)}-\frac1{(r+1)(r+2)}\right],
\]
Therefore
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac1{r(r+1)(r+2)}
=\frac12\left[
\frac1{1\cdot2}-\frac1{2\cdot3}
+\frac1{2\cdot3}-\frac1{3\cdot4}
+\cdots
+\frac1{n(n+1)}-\frac1{(n+1)(n+2)}
\right]
\]
\[
=\frac12\left(\frac12-\frac1{(n+1)(n+2)}\right),
\]
so
\[
\boxed{\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac1{r(r+1)(r+2)}
=\frac{n(n+3)}{4(n+1)(n+2)}}.
\]

 Completed

Sources: Cambridge International 9231/11/O/N/2021, Q2; 9231/13/O/N/2021, Q2.





2021 October/November · 9231/12 · Question 3 · 7 marks
Let
\[
S_n=\sum_{r=1}^{n}\ln\frac{r(r+2)}{(r+1)^2}.
\]
(a) Show that
\[
S_n=\ln\frac{n+2}{2(n+1)}.
\]
[4]
Let \(S\) be the corresponding sum to infinity.
(b) Find the least \(n\) for which \(S_n-S<0.01\). [3]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a) Write the summand as
\[
\ln r-2\ln(r+1)+\ln(r+2).
\]
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
S_n={}&(\ln1-2\ln2+\ln3)
+(\ln2-2\ln3+\ln4)+\cdots\\
&+(\ln n-2\ln(n+1)+\ln(n+2)).
\end{aligned}
\]
After cancellation,
\[
S_n=-\ln2-\ln(n+1)+\ln(n+2)
=\ln\frac{n+2}{2(n+1)}.
\]
(b) Taking \(n\to\infty\) gives
\[
S=\ln\frac12=-\ln2.
\]
Hence
\[
S_n-S=\ln\frac{n+2}{n+1}.
\]
We require
\[
\ln\frac{n+2}{n+1}<0.01
\]
Exponentiating,
\[
\frac{n+2}{n+1}<e^{0.01}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
n>\frac{2-e^{0.01}}{e^{0.01}-1}=98.5008\ldots.
\]
Therefore the least integer value is
\[
\boxed{n=99}.
\]

 Completed

Source: Cambridge International 9231/12/O/N/2021, Q3.




2022



2022 May/June · 9231/11 & 9231/12 · Question 1(a) · 4 marks
Let \(a\) be positive. Use the method of differences to find
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac1{(ar+1)(ar+a+1)}.
\]


Show answer and mark scheme

Partial fractions give
\[
\frac1{(ar+1)(ar+a+1)}
=\frac1a\left(\frac1{ar+1}-\frac1{ar+a+1}\right).
\]
Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac1{(ar+1)(ar+a+1)}
=\frac1a\bigg[&\left(\frac1{a+1}-\frac1{2a+1}\right)\\
&+\left(\frac1{2a+1}-\frac1{3a+1}\right)+\cdots\\
&+\left(\frac1{an+1}-\frac1{an+a+1}\right)\bigg].
\end{aligned}
\]
All intermediate terms cancel, so
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac1{(ar+1)(ar+a+1)}
=\frac1a\left(\frac1{a+1}-\frac1{an+a+1}\right),
\]
and therefore
\[
\boxed{\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac1{(ar+1)(ar+a+1)}
=\frac{n}{(a+1)(an+a+1)}}.
\]

 Completed

Sources: Cambridge International 9231/11/M/J/2022, Q1(a); 9231/12/M/J/2022, Q1(a).





2022 May/June · 9231/13 · Question 4 · 6 marks
Let
\[
u_r=e^{rx}(e^{2x}-2e^x+1).
\]
(a) Find \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}u_r\) in terms of \(n\) and \(x\). [3]
(b) Deduce the non-zero values of \(x\) for which the infinite series converges and give its sum. [3]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a) Since \(e^{2x}-2e^x+1=(e^x-1)^2\),
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}u_r
=(e^x-1)^2\sum_{r=1}^{n}e^{rx}.
\]
For \(x\ne0\), the geometric sum is
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}e^{rx}
=\frac{e^x(e^{nx}-1)}{e^x-1}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{\sum_{r=1}^{n}u_r=e^x(e^x-1)(e^{nx}-1)}.
\]
(b) Since \(x\ne0\), the only \(n\)-dependent factor is \(e^{nx}\). A finite limit exists precisely when \(e^{nx}\to0\), i.e. when \(x<0\). Then
\[
e^x(e^x-1)(e^{nx}-1)longrightarrow-e^x(e^x-1),
\]
so
\[
\boxed{\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}u_r=e^x(1-e^x)}.
\]

 Completed

Source: Cambridge International 9231/13/M/J/2022, Q4.




2023



2023 October/November · 9231/11 & 9231/13 · Question 1 · 7 marks
(a) By considering \((r+1)^2-r^2\), prove by the method of differences that
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}r=\frac12n(n+1).
\]
[4]
(b) Given \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}(r+a)=n^2\), find \(a\) in terms of \(n\). [3]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a) Since
\[
(r+1)^2-r^2=2r+1,
\]
summing from \(r=1\) to \(n\) gives
\[
(2^2-1^2)+(3^2-2^2)+\cdots+\{(n+1)^2-n^2\}
=2\sum_{r=1}^{n}r+n.
\]
The left side telescopes to \((n+1)^2-1\), so
\[
2\sum_{r=1}^{n}r=(n+1)^2-1-n=n(n+1).
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{\sum_{r=1}^{n}r=\frac12n(n+1)}.
\]
(b) Using part (a),
\[
\frac12n(n+1)+an=n^2,
\]
As \(n>0\), divide by \(n\):
\[
\frac{n+1}{2}+a=n.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{a=\frac{n-1}{2}}.
\]

 Completed

Sources: Cambridge International 9231/11/O/N/2023, Q1; 9231/13/O/N/2023, Q1.





2023 October/November · 9231/12 · Question 1 · 8 marks
(a) Find \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}(3r^2+3r+1)\). [3]
(b) Show that
\[
\frac1{r^3}-\frac1{(r+1)^3}
=\frac{3r^2+3r+1}{r^3(r+1)^3},
\]
and hence find the corresponding sum from \(r=1\) to \(n\). [5]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a)
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}(3r^2+3r+1)
=3\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}6
+3\frac{n(n+1)}2+n
\]
\[
=n^3+3n^2+3n
=\boxed{(n+1)^3-1}.
\]
(b) Combining the left side of the stated identity,
\[
\frac1{r^3}-\frac1{(r+1)^3}
=\frac{(r+1)^3-r^3}{r^3(r+1)^3}
=\frac{3r^2+3r+1}{r^3(r+1)^3}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac{3r^2+3r+1}{r^3(r+1)^3}
=\left(1-\frac1{2^3}\right)
+\left(\frac1{2^3}-\frac1{3^3}\right)+\cdots
+\left(\frac1{n^3}-\frac1{(n+1)^3}\right).
\]
The intermediate terms cancel, giving
\[
\boxed{\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac{3r^2+3r+1}{r^3(r+1)^3}
=1-\frac1{(n+1)^3}}.
\]

 Completed

Source: Cambridge International 9231/12/O/N/2023, Q1.




2024



2024 May/June · 9231/11 & 9231/12 · Question 3 · 7 marks
(a) Use standard results to show that
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{N}r(r+1)(3r+4)
=\frac1{12}N(N+1)(N+2)(9N+19).
\]
[3]
(b) Express \((3r+4)/[r(r+1)]\) in partial fractions and hence find
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{N}\frac{3r+4}{r(r+1)}\left(\frac14\right)^{r+1}.
\]
[4]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a) Expanding,
\[
r(r+1)(3r+4)=3r^3+7r^2+4r.
\]
Hence
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{N}r(r+1)(3r+4)
=3\left\{\frac{N(N+1)}2\right\}^2
+\frac76N(N+1)(2N+1)+2N(N+1)
\]
\[
=\frac1{12}N(N+1)(9N^2+37N+38)
\]
\[
=\boxed{\frac1{12}N(N+1)(N+2)(9N+19)}.
\]
(b) Partial fractions give
\[
\frac{3r+4}{r(r+1)}=\frac4r-\frac1{r+1}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\frac{3r+4}{r(r+1)}\left(\frac14\right)^{r+1}
=\frac1{r4^r}-\frac1{(r+1)4^{r+1}}.
\]
The sum is
\[
\left(\frac14-\frac1{2\cdot4^2}\right)
+\left(\frac1{2\cdot4^2}-\frac1{3\cdot4^3}\right)
+\cdots
+\left(\frac1{N4^N}-\frac1{(N+1)4^{N+1}}\right).
\]
Consecutive terms cancel, giving
\[
\boxed{\sum_{r=1}^{N}\frac{3r+4}{r(r+1)}\left(\frac14\right)^{r+1}
=\frac14-\frac1{(N+1)4^{N+1}}}.
\]

 Completed

Sources: Cambridge International 9231/11/M/J/2024, Q3; 9231/12/M/J/2024, Q3.





2024 October/November · 9231/11 & 9231/13 · Question 4 · 8 marks
Let \(k\) be a positive constant.
(a) Use the method of differences to find
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac{5k}{(5r+k)(5r+5+k)}.
\]
[4]
(b) It is given that the corresponding infinite series has sum \(1/3\). Find \(k\). [2]
(c) Hence find
\[
\sum_{r=n}^{n^2}\frac{5k}{(5r+k)(5r+5+k)}.
\]
[2]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a) Partial fractions give
\[
\frac{5k}{(5r+k)(5r+5+k)}
=k\left(\frac1{5r+k}-\frac1{5r+5+k}\right).
\]
Thus
\[
k\left[
\left(\frac1{5+k}-\frac1{10+k}\right)
+\left(\frac1{10+k}-\frac1{15+k}\right)+\cdots
+\left(\frac1{5n+k}-\frac1{5n+5+k}\right)
\right].
\]
After cancellation,
\[
\boxed{\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac{5k}{(5r+k)(5r+5+k)}
=k\left(\frac1{5+k}-\frac1{5n+5+k}\right)}.
\]
(b) Letting \(n\to\infty\) in part (a), the infinite sum is
\[
\frac{k}{5+k}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\frac{k}{5+k}=\frac13
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
3k=5+k.
\]
Hence \(\boxed{k=5/2}\).
(c) For \(k=5/2\), the summand becomes
\[
\frac1{2r+1}-\frac1{2r+3}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\sum_{r=n}^{n^2}\left(\frac1{2r+1}-\frac1{2r+3}\right)
=\left(\frac1{2n+1}-\frac1{2n+3}\right)+\cdots
+\left(\frac1{2n^2+1}-\frac1{2n^2+3}\right),
\]
so
\[
\boxed{\sum_{r=n}^{n^2}\frac{5k}{(5r+k)(5r+5+k)}
=\frac1{2n+1}-\frac1{2n^2+3}}.
\]

 Completed

Sources: Cambridge International 9231/11/O/N/2024, Q4; 9231/13/O/N/2024, Q4.





2024 October/November · 9231/12 · Question 5 · 9 marks
It is given that
\[
S_n=\sum_{r=1}^{n}u_r,
\qquad
u_r=x^{f(r)}-x^{f(r+1)},
\qquad x>0.
\]
(a) Find \(S_n\) in terms of \(n,x\) and \(f\). [2]
(b) For \(f(r)=\ln r\), determine when the infinite series converges and give its sum. [3]
(c) For \(f(r)=2\log_x r\), \(x\ne1\), find \(\sum_{n=1}^{N}S_n\) in fully factorised form. [4]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a) The defining difference telescopes:
\[
\begin{aligned}
S_n={}&\{x^{f(1)}-x^{f(2)}\}
+\{x^{f(2)}-x^{f(3)}\}+\cdots\\
&+\{x^{f(n)}-x^{f(n+1)}\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{S_n=x^{f(1)}-x^{f(n+1)}}.
\]
(b) For \(f(r)=\ln r\),
\[
x^{f(r)}=x^{\ln r}=r^{\ln x}.
\]
Since \(f(1)=0\),
\[
S_n=1-(n+1)^{\ln x}.
\]
If \(0<x<1\), then \(\ln x<0\) and \((n+1)^{\ln x}\to0\), so the sum is \(1\). If \(x=1\), every term is zero and the sum is \(0\). If \(x>1\), then \(\ln x>0\) and the partial sums have no finite limit. Thus the series converges for \(0<x\le1\), with the two sums stated above.
(c) For \(f(r)=2\log_x r\) and \(x\ne1\),
\[
x^{f(r)}=x^{2\log_x r}=r^2,
\]
so
\[
S_n=1-(n+1)^2=-n(n+2).
\]
Therefore
\[
\sum_{n=1}^{N}S_n
=-\sum_{n=1}^{N}(n^2+2n)
=-\frac{N(N+1)(2N+1)}6-N(N+1)
\]
and hence
\[
\boxed{\sum_{n=1}^{N}S_n=-\frac16N(N+1)(2N+7)}.
\]

 Completed

Source: Cambridge International 9231/12/O/N/2024, Q5.




2025



2025 May/June · 9231/11 & 9231/12 · Question 1 · 7 marks
(a) Use standard results to show that
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}(2-3r)(5-3r)=an^3+bn^2+cn,
\]
and find the integers \(a,b,c\). [3]
(b) Use the method of differences to find
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac1{(2-3r)(5-3r)}.
\]
[4]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a) Expanding,
\[
(2-3r)(5-3r)=9r^2-21r+10.
\]
Therefore
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}(2-3r)(5-3r)
=9\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}6
-21\frac{n(n+1)}2+10n
\]
\[
=3n^3-6n^2+n.
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{a=3,\quad b=-6,\quad c=1}.
\]
(b) Partial fractions give
\[
\frac1{(2-3r)(5-3r)}
=\frac13\left(\frac1{2-3r}-\frac1{5-3r}\right).
\]
Writing the terms,
\[
\frac13\left[
\left(-1-\frac12\right)
+\left(-\frac14+1\right)
+\left(-\frac17+\frac14\right)
+\cdots
+\left(\frac1{2-3n}-\frac1{5-3n}\right)
\right].
\]
Since \(5-3r=2-3(r-1)\), the intermediate terms cancel. The remaining expression is
\[
\frac13\left(\frac1{2-3n}-\frac12\right)
=\frac{n}{2(2-3n)}.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac1{(2-3r)(5-3r)}
=\frac{n}{2(2-3n)}}.
\]

 Completed

Sources: Cambridge International 9231/11/M/J/2025, Q1; 9231/12/M/J/2025, Q1.





2025 May/June · 9231/14 · Question 1 · 6 marks
(a) Find \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}(2r+1)\). [2]
(b) Show that
\[
\frac{2r+1}{(r^2+1)(r^2+2r+2)}
=\frac1{r^2+1}-\frac1{r^2+2r+2}.
\]
[1]
(c) Hence find the corresponding sum from \(r=1\) to \(n\). [2]
(d) Deduce the sum to infinity. [1]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a)
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}(2r+1)
=2\frac{n(n+1)}2+n
=\boxed{n(n+2)}.
\]
(b) Since \(r^2+2r+2=(r+1)^2+1\),
\[
\frac1{r^2+1}-\frac1{r^2+2r+2}
=\frac{(r^2+2r+2)-(r^2+1)}{(r^2+1)(r^2+2r+2)}
\]
\[
=\frac{2r+1}{(r^2+1)(r^2+2r+2)},
\]
as required.
(c) Therefore the sum is
\[
\left(\frac12-\frac15\right)
+\left(\frac15-\frac1{10}\right)+\cdots
+\left(\frac1{n^2+1}-\frac1{(n+1)^2+1}\right).
\]
The intermediate terms cancel, giving
\[
\boxed{\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac{2r+1}{(r^2+1)(r^2+2r+2)}
=\frac12-\frac1{(n+1)^2+1}}.
\]
(d) Since \(1/\{(n+1)^2+1\}\to0\), the sum to infinity is \(\boxed{\frac12}\).

 Completed

Source: Cambridge International 9231/14/M/J/2025, Q1.





2025 October/November · 9231/11 & 9231/13 · Question 1 · 9 marks
(a) Find
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}(8r^3+12r^2+4r+3).
\]
[3]
(b) Show that
\[
\frac1{r^4}-\frac1{(r+1)^4}
=\frac{4r^3+6r^2+4r+1}{r^4(r+1)^4},
\]
and hence find the corresponding sum to \(n\). [5]
(c) Deduce the sum to infinity. [1]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a) Using the standard formulae,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{r=1}^{n}(8r^3+12r^2+4r+3)
={}&8\left\{\frac{n(n+1)}2\right\}^2\\
&+2n(n+1)(2n+1)+2n(n+1)+3n.
\end{aligned}
\]
Collecting and factorising gives
\[
\boxed{\sum_{r=1}^{n}(8r^3+12r^2+4r+3)
=n(2n^3+8n^2+10n+7)}.
\]
(b) First,
\[
\frac1{r^4}-\frac1{(r+1)^4}
=\frac{(r+1)^4-r^4}{r^4(r+1)^4}
=\frac{4r^3+6r^2+4r+1}{r^4(r+1)^4},
\]
as required. Hence
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac{4r^3+6r^2+4r+1}{r^4(r+1)^4}
=\left(1-\frac1{2^4}\right)
+\left(\frac1{2^4}-\frac1{3^4}\right)+\cdots
+\left(\frac1{n^4}-\frac1{(n+1)^4}\right).
\]
The intermediate terms cancel, so
\[
\boxed{\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac{4r^3+6r^2+4r+1}{r^4(r+1)^4}
=1-\frac1{(n+1)^4}}.
\]
(c) Since \(1/(n+1)^4\to0\), the sum to infinity is \(\boxed{1}\).

 Completed

Sources: Cambridge International 9231/11/O/N/2025, Q1; 9231/13/O/N/2025, Q1.





2025 October/November · 9231/12 · Question 1 · 9 marks
(a) Find \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}(r^3-r)\) in fully factorised form. [3]
(b) Express
\[
\frac{r+3}{r^3-r}
\]
as \(A/(r-1)+B/r+C/(r+1)\), and hence find its sum from \(r=2\) to \(n\). [5]
(c) Deduce the sum to infinity. [1]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a)
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}(r^3-r)
=\left\{\frac{n(n+1)}2\right\}^2-\frac{n(n+1)}2
\]
\[
=\frac14n(n+1)\{n(n+1)-2\}
=\boxed{\frac14n(n-1)(n+1)(n+2)}.
\]
(b) Since \(r^3-r=(r-1)r(r+1)\), set
\[
\frac{r+3}{(r-1)r(r+1)}
=\frac{A}{r-1}+\frac Br+\frac C{r+1}.
\]
Multiplying through by \((r-1)r(r+1)\) gives
\[
r+3=Ar(r+1)+B(r-1)(r+1)+Cr(r-1).
\]
Using \(r=1,0,-1\) gives \(A=2\), \(B=-3\), \(C=1\). Thus
\[
\frac{r+3}{r^3-r}=\frac2{r-1}-\frac3r+\frac1{r+1}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{r=2}^{n}\frac{r+3}{r^3-r}
={}&\left(2-\frac32+\frac13\right)
+\left(1-1+\frac14\right)+\cdots\\
&+\left(\frac2{n-1}-\frac3n+\frac1{n+1}\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
Collecting the uncancelled terms gives
\[
\boxed{\sum_{r=2}^{n}\frac{r+3}{r^3-r}
=\frac32-\frac2n+\frac1{n+1}}.
\]
(c) Letting \(n\to\infty\), the two remaining \(n\)-dependent fractions tend to zero, so the sum to infinity is \(\boxed{\frac32}\).

 Completed

Source: Cambridge International 9231/12/O/N/2025, Q1.





2025 October/November · 9231/14 · Question 3 · 9 marks
(a) Use standard results to show that
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}(r+1)(r+2)(r+3)
=\frac14n(n^3+bn^2+cn+d),
\]
and determine \(b,c,d\). [3]
(b) Express \(2/[(r+1)(r+2)(r+3)]\) in partial fractions and hence find its sum from \(r=1\) to \(n\). [5]
(c) State the sum to infinity. [1]


Show answer and mark scheme

(a) Expand the summand:
\[
(r+1)(r+2)(r+3)=r^3+6r^2+11r+6.
\]
Hence
\[
\sum_{r=1}^{n}(r+1)(r+2)(r+3)
=\left\{\frac{n(n+1)}2\right\}^2
+n(n+1)(2n+1)
+\frac{11}{2}n(n+1)+6n
\]
\[
=\frac14n(n^3+10n^2+35n+50).
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{b=10,\quad c=35,\quad d=50}.
\]
(b) Use
\[
\frac2{(r+1)(r+2)(r+3)}
=\frac1{(r+1)(r+2)}-\frac1{(r+2)(r+3)}.
\]
Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac2{(r+1)(r+2)(r+3)}
={}&\left(\frac1{2\cdot3}-\frac1{3\cdot4}\right)\\
&+\left(\frac1{3\cdot4}-\frac1{4\cdot5}\right)+\cdots\\
&+\left(\frac1{(n+1)(n+2)}-\frac1{(n+2)(n+3)}\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
After cancellation,
\[
\boxed{\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac2{(r+1)(r+2)(r+3)}
=\frac16-\frac1{(n+2)(n+3)}}.
\]
(c) The final fraction tends to zero, so the sum to infinity is \(\boxed{\frac16}\).

 Completed

Source: Cambridge International 9231/14/O/N/2025, Q3.
